Tuning range, response targets, adjustment method and test conditions Applications requiring an evaluated tuning function View parameters Submit custom Waveguide filter Do the frequency, waveguide interface and mechanical constraints call for a waveguide structure? Passband, rejection, power, waveguide size, flange and envelope E-band and other high-frequency custom projects View parameters Submit custom Custom filter assembly Must filtering be integrated with a custom mechanical or multi-part assembly? System function, RF targets, drawings, interfaces and validation plan Custom RF/microwave assemblies and application-specific integration View parameters Submit custom Images identify product forms, not unsupported insertion-loss, rejection or power ratings. Available documents and custom feasibility are confirmed against the exact model or project. 02 / Bandpass response 6 terms · one measured curve Read the Bandpass Filter Response before Comparing Structures A bandpass filter passes a defined band and rejects frequencies below and above it. Each term below describes that curve, and each one needs a frequency reference and a test condition before it can be quoted or verified. Response terms apply to cavity, waveguide and assembly-level bandpass designs alike. Response term What it describes What to state Passband edges The frequencies the filter must pass Lower and upper edges, with the loss level used to define them Bandwidth The width of the passband Minimum bandwidth across the operating condition Insertion loss Loss through the passband Maximum loss across the band, with the reference plane stated Rejection Attenuation below and above the passband Each stopband interval and its minimum attenuation Return loss Match at each port across the passband Value per port and the frequency range Power and PIM What the filter carries and what it must not generate Power type and level; PIM limit, tones, order and test setup where applicable A bandpass filter is one response shape among several: a lowpass passes below a corner, a highpass above it, and a notch rejects a narrow band. The structure follows the response, not the other way round. When separate bands are routed to separate ports, the device is a diplexer; the RF diplexer guide covers guard band, isolation and power inputs. For the structural comparison, read the cavity vs waveguide filter selection guide ; for the complete input list, use the RF filter RFQ preparation checklist . 03 / Selection ledger 3 approaches · 9 review dimensions Choose between Cavity, Waveguide and Tuning-Free Filter Approaches Cavity and waveguide describe structural paths. Tuning-free is a manufacturing and adjustment objective. These labels are not three mutually exclusive product branches. Selection dimension Cavity structure Waveguide structure Tuning-free objective Operating frequency Define the exact passband and rejection bands. Confirm band, waveguide interface and high-frequency feasibility. Confirm the frequency range over which adjustment must be avoided. Insertion-loss target Evaluate with resonator, coupling and response requirements. Evaluate with waveguide structure, finish and reference plane. Include variation across the agreed production condition. Out-of-band rejection Specify frequencies and minimum rejection together. Include spurious or out-of-band conditions relevant to the system. Define allowable variation without manual adjustment. Power State power level, type and operating conditions. Include interface, environment and power-test conditions. Insertion loss varies with path length and frequency; the accepted value for a specific build is the one measured on the delivered unit. Confirm the datasheet revision before design freeze. Send a Port Map See Matrices in Test Systems 02 / Specification 4 levers Four Values Settle Most Matrix Projects Frequency range, path count, isolation and power handling are coupled. Raising one usually moves the others, so they are reviewed together rather than quoted one at a time. Lever 01 Frequency range The band sets switch type, connector series and path layout. Wideband coverage to 18 GHz is available, but loss and isolation are specified at defined points, not as one flat figure. Lever 02 Path count and topology Fan-out accepts one common port and many branches. A full matrix needs a crosspoint at every intersection, so cost and loss rise faster than the port count. Lever 03 Isolation Isolation decides whether an unselected path can disturb the measurement. Published values range from 60 dB to 70 dB depending on configuration and band. Lever 04 Power and control Solid-state switches suit low-level measurement paths; the 8×8 configuration is rated to 20 dBm. Control is by the test software over the interface agreed at review. Where a project needs higher power than a solid-state path allows, a different switch technology or a relay-based design is reviewed instead. That decision is made before the enclosure and control board are released. 03 / Signal path 5 nodes From Instrument Port to Device Under Test The signal path is short by design. Every added node contributes loss, mismatch and a calibration step, so the chain is drawn before the hardware is built. Instrument port The analyzer or source connects at the common port. Port count and connector series are confirmed against the instrument. Input routing Internal cabling and the first switch stage set the loss floor. Cable lengths are matched where phase matters. Switch core Solid-state switches select the path. Switching time, isolation and power rating are properties of this stage. Output field Outputs land on a labelled connector field — A1–A8 and B1–B8 on the 8×8 unit — so the port map is readable at the rack. Control and calibration The control interface is driven by the test software. Path loss and phase are characterized during integration so limits can be set per path. Rack units across the matrix family. Front-panel port labels follow the customer port map, not a fixed numbering. Multi-port switch module. Internal assembly, connector field and control board are built as one replaceable unit. 04 / Integration 3 checks What the Integration Review Covers A matrix is rarely bought alone. It is accepted as part of a measurement chain, and the chain is what determines whether the published isolation still holds at the device. Integration checks before a switch matrix is accepted into a measurement chain. Check What is reviewed Why it matters Cabling and connectors Connector series, torque access, cable bend radius and rack depth A poor cable route can add more loss and mismatch than the matrix itself Path calibration Per-path loss and phase, stored and applied by the software Limits set against an uncalibrated path will pass or fail the wrong units Control sequence Switching order, settling time and instrument handshake Reading before the path settles produces intermittent, hard-to-trace failures Where the matrix is supplied with a test system, these checks are part of system acceptance. Where it is supplied as a standalone unit, the interface and calibration method are documented so the customer can repeat them. 05 / RFQ inputs 2 stages What a Matrix Quote Needs Topology, band and port map decide most of the build. Sending them together shortens the review from several exchanges to one. Send a Power and Band See RF Accessories 02 / Thermal path 3 blocks Where High-Power Passives Fail A 200 W attenuator is a thermal component that happens to have an RF function. Heat has to leave the resistive element and reach the housing before it reaches the connector. Block 01 Resistive element Thin-film or thick-film on a thermally conductive substrate. The element geometry sets both the attenuation value and the heat density it must survive. Block 02 Die attach and substrate The die attachment and substrate carry heat into the metal housing. A void here shows up later as drift or an open circuit under load. Block 03 Housing and fins Machined housing with fins or a mounting pad. The interface to the bench or cold plate is part of the rating and is stated on the datasheet. High-power termination. The heat sink is sized for continuous dissipation at the rated ambient, not for short bursts. Eight-way microstrip divider in a machined housing. Isolation depends on the internal termination quality, not only the split ratio. Linear performance matters as much as thermal performance. pages.text_excerpt: Home Products RF Front-Ends RF front-ends · 13 channels · 6–18 GHz Ku-Band Multi-Channel RF Front-Ends, 6–18 GHz A 13-channel receive front-end with protected low-noise amplification, switched delay and per-channel attenuation for wideband arrays and instrumentation. The reference build below is a starting point; channel count, band and control word are re-cut for the platform. Specify a Front-End Review the Specification Plate 05 13-channel Ku 13-channel Ku-band front-end housing with SMPM connectors. Channels share one control interface and one thermal path. Channels 13 Band 6–18 GHz Gain 40.5 ± 1.5 dB Noise figure ≤4 dB 01 / Reference build 11 values Reference Build: 13 Channels, 6–18 GHz These are the published values for the reference front-end. They define what the platform can do before a project changes the channel count or the band. Published values for the 13-channel Ku-band RF front-end reference build. Parameter Published value Notes Channel count 13 Channels share one control interface and one housing Frequency range 6–18 GHz Wideband receive coverage across Ku and lower bands Noise figure ≤4 dB, 4.5 dB over temperature Specified at the front-end input Gain 40.5 ± 1.5 dB Channel-to-channel gain spread inside the stated window Amplitude tracking ±1 dB Across channels at matched attenuation states Phase tracking ±10° Across channels; the delay states add their own quantization Switched delay 1λ at 12 GHz, 6-bit Delay range and step are set by the 12 GHz reference Attenuation ≥31 dB range, 1 dB step Applied per channel for amplitude taper Channel isolation ≥50 dB Between adjacent channels in the same housing Input burn-out ≥10 W Protection level at the input without damage Power and cooling 12 V, ≤10 W, natural convection to +55 °C No forced air in the reference build Values are the source specification for this build. Any change to channel count, band or housing changes the thermal case and usually the gain budget, so the table is re-issued for the ordered variant rather than carried over unchanged. Send a Platform Requirement Review T/R Modules 02 / Signal chain 6 stages Six Stages Between the Antenna and the Receiver Each stage exists to protect a downstream one. The order is not arbitrary: protection comes before amplification, and delay comes after the noise figure is set. Input protection Limits the level that reaches the first amplifier. The burn-out rating of at least 10 W is the level the input survives without damage. Low-noise amplification Sets the noise figure for the whole chain. Published at ≤4 dB, rising to 4.5 dB across the temperature range. Switched delay Adds a 6-bit delay covering one wavelength at 12 GHz. Delay is applied after the noise figure is fixed so the switch loss does not sit in front of the LNA. Per-channel attenuation Applies amplitude taper at a 1 dB step over at least 31 dB. Attenuation states are used for tracking and for taper, not as a substitute for level control elsewhere. Gain and distribution Brings each channel to 40.5 ± 1.5 dB at the output and routes it to the connector field. Control interface Carries channel settings for delay and attenuation. The control word is agreed with the beam controller before layout. What the numbers mean together Gain, noise figure and tracking are specified together because they compete. Adding gain in front of the delay improves the noise figure but increases the power the switch must handle; increasing attenuation range reduces the output level available for the receiver. The gain budget is agreed as one set of values, not parameter by parameter. Delay quantization matters as well: a 6-bit delay creates phase steps that appear as residual phase error after beam steering. The step size and the resulting error at the operating frequency are stated with the datasheet so the digitization can be judged against the array requirement. At review Channel count and channel spacing Band and the delay reference frequency Gain budget and noise-figure target Delay range, step and quantization limit Attenuation range and step Input protection level Housing, connector field and cooling The reference build is natural convection to +55 °C. A higher ambient or a sealed housing changes the thermal path and is quoted separately. 03 / Validation 5 checkpoints How a Front-End Is Accepted Acceptance is agreed in writing before the first article. Tracking and delay quantization are measured, not inferred from component data. Front-end acceptance checkpoints and what each one verifies. Checkpoint Method What it verifies Gain and match S-parameters per channel across 6–18 GHz Gain window and input match at the connector Noise figure Noise measurement per channel at ambient and at temperature Both the ≤4 dB and the 4.5 dB over-temperature values Tracking Amplitude and phase across all 13 channels at matched states The ±1 dB and ±10° windows the array assumes Delay states Step response across all 6-bit delay states Range, step and quantization against the array limit Protection Input level applied at the burn-out rating That the protection survives the stated level without damage Environmental qualification beyond the stated operating temperature is quoted per project against the test standards in the requirement. This page does not publish a qualification claim for every build. 04 / RFQ inputs 2 stages What a Front-End Quote Needs Channel count, band and delay requirement decide the architecture. The housing and the connector field follow, and they set the thermal limit. Known at inquiry Channel count and channel spacing Band and delay reference frequency Gain and noise-figure targets Delay range, step and allowed quantization Attenuation range and step Input protection level Connector series and housing envelope Ambient and cooling condition Confirmed by review Channel layout, delay line design, attenuation stage and thermal path are confirmed against the housing and the beam controller. Price, lead time, warranty and acceptance tests are quoted per configuration and per order. This page does not publish a cross-project policy for any of them. A complete RFQ typically receives initial engineering feedback in about 24 hours; that response is not a final specification. Submit a Front-End RFQ Review Test and Quality 05 / Questions 5 entries RF Front-End Questions Five questions asked before a multichannel front-end is specified. Is the noise figure specified at ambient only? No. The reference build publishes ≤4 dB at ambient and 4.5 dB across the operating temperature range. Both values are measured, because a receiver budget built only on the room-temperature figure will be optimistic at the top of the range. Why is the delay referenced to 12 GHz? One wavelength of delay is a physical length, so a delay range quoted in wavelengths needs a reference frequency. At 12 GHz one wavelength corresponds to a defined time delay; the same hardware produces a different number of wavelengths at another frequency. The reference is stated so the range can be converted correctly. Does attenuation affect the noise figure? Attenuation is applied after the low-noise stage in this architecture, so it reduces output level without directly setting the input noise figure. The exact effect depends on where the attenuation sits relative to the gain stages, and that placement is shown on the block diagram issued with the datasheet. Can the channel count change from 13? Yes. Thirteen channels is the reference build. Channel count changes the housing, the control board and the thermal path, so it is fixed before layout. The gain and tracking budgets are re-issued for the new count rather than scaled from this table. What input level can it survive? The published burn-out rating is at least 10 W at the input, with protection ahead of the first amplifier. pages.text_excerpt: Home Engineering & Quality Testing & Quality VNA · PIM · Reliability · Matrix automation RF Testing and Quality Verification Buyers Can Audit Test evidence that connects the product and revision to the conditions, measured data, acceptance limit, lot or serial record and corrective action. The aim is a result your SQE can interpret, not a pass label without context. VNA S-parameters and applicable RF limits PIM Passive intermodulation by agreed setup Reliability Project-defined environmental or endurance checks Matrix Multi-port automated data capture ISO 9001 is presented as the quality-system fact. It is separate from the test evidence for a specific product and does not certify product performance. Request Sample Test Report Define Your Test Requirements Technician testing an RF filter with bench instruments. The photograph shows the test environment; it is not a report or a measured result. Match Each Test Method to the Question It Answers More test columns do not automatically mean more confidence. Each method needs a defined question, a test condition and an acceptance rule before its data can support a release decision. Test capability matrix: what each method demonstrates, the conditions it needs and its applicable boundary. Method Question it answers Required conditions Evidence output Applicable boundary VNA / S-parameters Do insertion loss, return loss, rejection or isolation meet the agreed limits? Frequency range, ports, impedance, sweep, calibration and setup conditions Curves or numerical data with product, revision, conditions and acceptance decision Parameters and samples defined by the verification plan; not every characteristic is covered PIM Does passive intermodulation meet the project limit under the stated configuration? Applicable bands, test power, tone or signal arrangement, ports, connection setup and limit Result with configuration, units and sample or lot linkage A dBc value is not comparable without its product and test conditions Reliability Does the product meet a specified environmental or endurance requirement? Test item, conditions, duration or cycles, sample size and before/after acceptance Condition record, performance comparison and disposition Only project-defined tests are included; no unconfirmed salt-spray or EMC claim is implied Matrix automation Can multi-port data be captured in a defined sequence with consistent records? Port map, switching sequence, measurement list, setup and reporting rules Multi-port or batch record linked to product, ports and test steps Automation does not mean every test or every unit is covered Method boundary: VNA, PIM, reliability and matrix automation are capability areas. The actual test plan, sample size and acceptance criteria are agreed for the product and project. A photograph of the setup helps orientation but cannot replace the condition record and result data. Buyer check before accepting a result Is the product and revision the one you are approving? Do the test conditions match the specification? Is the acceptance limit stated with units? Does the reported lot or serial match the delivered hardware? Is a deviation identified, or is it hidden inside an average? The sample report used in a review is redacted. Field labels and blank values are intentional; no customer name, fabricated curve or invented measurement is added to illustrate the format. Route Typical input Process Key control Output record CNC milling Cavity, cover, housing or heatsink drawing Multi-axis milling, drilling and profiling Datum consistency, wall thickness, critical dimensions and surface condition Machining record, dimensional inspection and revision link CNC turning Connector body, flange or rotationally symmetric part Turning, boring, threading and parting Concentricity, thread form, face squareness and finish Dimensional record tied to the lot and drawing revision Sheet metal Cabinet, bracket, panel or enclosure drawing Laser cutting, forming, bending and hardware insertion Flat pattern, bend allowance, hole position and assembly fit First-article and assembly check records Surface finishing Material, masked areas and finish specification Pre-treatment, plating or coating Functional surface, thickness target and appearance criteria Finish record and applicable thickness verification Assembly and test Parts, fasteners, tuning and test requirements Assembly, fastening, tuning and RF verification Build revision, fastener control, test setup and acceptance limit Build record, test data and lot or serial traceability Operator loading parts at a CNC machining center. Review Manufacturing Inputs See enclosure manufacturing context → Tolerance, Plating and Surface-Control Evidence A tolerance statement becomes useful only when the drawing characteristic, applicable structure, measurement method and record are defined together. The figures below are conditional capabilities, not blanket guarantees. Feature, condition, method and record for high-frequency tolerance and plating review. Feature and condition Capability statement Measurement method Record expected Critical cavity dimension above 40 GHz Can reach ±0.01 mm for suitable structures Drawing-defined dimensional inspection with an agreed datum scheme Measured value, method, revision and disposition Plating thickness above 60 GHz Can reach 1 μm control for suitable designs Agreed thickness measurement on the specified functional surface Surface requirement, result and acceptance status Mating face and flange Flatness and alignment reviewed against the interface requirement Surface or assembly check using the project method Inspection record and fit result Exterior or appearance surface Finish defined by material, pre-treatment and coating specification Visual and finish record against agreed criteria Finish record and any approved deviation Precision CNC machining of high-frequency parts. The process supports the capability discussion; the final requirement belongs on the controlled drawing. Reading a tolerance or plating record Which drawing characteristic and revision the value belongs to Which datum scheme and measurement location were used Which method or instrument produced the result Whether the value is a capability statement or an inspection result What deviation, if any, was accepted and by whom Measurement records are redacted for review; customer drawings and names are not published. Where a result depends on a specific instrument, fixture or sample location, that condition is stated with the value rather than separated from it. The connection to RF evidence is defined separately: geometry and plating records support the hardware definition, while VNA, PIM or reliability results provide performance evidence for the agreed test plan. Conditional capability: ±0.01 mm and 1 μm are not universal figures. They apply only to suitable structures, within the stated frequency contexts, and require a drawing requirement plus an agreed verification method. Review Verification Evidence See test report fields → Assembly, Tuning and RF Verification Machined parts become an RF assembly through incoming checks, controlled fastening, tuning and test. Each step should leave a record that points back to the build revision and forward to the acceptance decision. Step 01 · Incoming and assembly Part condition and build Check received parts against the revision, then assemble with the specified fasteners, torque or fixture requirements. Record any fit or surface finding before closing the unit. pages.text_excerpt: Home Engineering & Quality NPI Prototype · First article · Pilot run · Controlled release From Prototype to Pilot Run to Repeatable Mass Production A structured NPI path for RF components and precision structures. Each stage answers a different risk question, produces its own record and ends at a gate where the next decision is made. 01 Prototype 02 First Article 03 Pilot Run 04 Release The evidence chain links controlled drawings and BOM, FAI, pilot findings, test baselines and engineering changes. A passed sample does not by itself release production. Plan Your NPI Path Review FAI Requirements RF component production line. The photograph shows production equipment, not a yield figure, customer program or delivery timeline. Separate Prototype, First Article, Pilot and Production Objectives The same part can be physically present at every stage while the evidence is completely different. Compare the intended decision, not just the hardware, before moving a project forward. NPI stage comparison: purpose, inputs, review points, exit condition and what each stage cannot prove. Stage Purpose Inputs Review points Exit condition What it does not prove Prototype Test the design concept against agreed targets Design version, sample target and proposed test conditions RF and mechanical function, assembly feasibility and observed deviations Prototype results and deviations have a documented conclusion Repeatability, process control or production readiness First Article Verify the controlled definition produces a conforming part Controlled drawing and BOM, material and finish requirements Critical dimensions, material and surface, assembly and applicable RF tests FAI record and deviation status accepted or dispositioned Stable output across a production run Pilot Run Evaluate the proposed process and evidence baseline First-article disposition, draft process and draft test baseline Repeatability, assembly and tuning, test coverage and issue closure Pilot summary and production open-item list with owners That every future lot will match the pilot Controlled Production Produce against the approved baseline with defined controls Approved drawing, BOM, process, inspection and change interface Production, inspection, traceability and change control according to plan Production records retained against the released baseline That all risk has disappeared or that delivery dates are fixed Comparison boundary: The table is a planning framework. Participants, record formats and exit criteria are agreed for the product and project; no universal NPI calendar is implied. Compare Your Current NPI Stage Define the test evidence → Use Stage Gates to Control NPI Release Decisions A gate is a decision record, not a meeting title. Each role contributes its own evidence, and unresolved items need an owner and a disposition before the next stage starts. G0 NPI Kickoff Buyer / R&D Confirm specification revision, quantity stage and target validation milestone. Engineering Identify missing inputs, assumptions and the review scope. Quality / Manufacturing Flag inspection, process and capacity questions early. Exit: gate plan, owners and data-gap list. G1 Prototype Exit Buyer / R&D Confirm whether the agreed prototype acceptance targets are met. Engineering Compare measured results with targets and record deviations. Quality / Manufacturing Review DFM and assembly risks before a first article is planned. Exit: deviation list and a first-article decision. G2 FAI / Pilot Exit Buyer / R&D Review deviations and any project-specific approval points. Engineering Assess RF and mechanical deltas against the baseline. Quality / Manufacturing Check inspection, traceability, process and assembly findings. Exit: open-item disposition and a release recommendation. G3 Production Release Buyer / R&D Confirm the approved revision and change interface for the project. Engineering Verify the drawing, BOM, process and test baseline are aligned. Quality / Manufacturing Confirm inspection, traceability and records are defined. Exit: approved production baseline. Residual risk is recorded, not erased. Open-item rule: Every unresolved finding needs a stated impact, owner, planned action and whether it blocks release. A gate can pass with open items when that disposition is explicitly accepted. pages.text_excerpt: Home Resources RFQ Guide RFQ checklist · Band plans · Verification inputs How to Prepare an RFQ Engineers Can Quote Directly An actionable quotation starts with a specification an engineer can review. This checklist organizes the frequency, performance, interface, mechanical, environmental, quantity and verification fields that belong in a custom RF, waveguide or enclosure RFQ. Frequency and bandwidth Insertion loss Rejection and isolation Power PIM Connectors Mechanical envelope Environment Quantity Verification A complete RFQ typically receives initial engineering feedback in about 24 hours. That feedback is not a formal quotation, a prototype commitment or a production lead-time promise. Submit Complete RFQ Open the Copyable Checklist Drawing review at SONNE. The image documents the review environment, not a quotation, test result or customer project. RF Specification Checklist Every value should carry a unit, a test condition and a note on whether it is mandatory or a target. A model number or a single frequency rarely defines a custom part. Units, conditions and priority Insertion loss without band edges or a return-loss reference cannot be compared between suppliers. State whether each limit applies across the full band, at a single frequency or at a temperature extreme, and group the fields by priority. Required: values the design cannot be reviewed without. Target: desirable performance used to compare options. TBD: not yet known, so engineering can flag the missing input instead of guessing. PIM and rejection need their own context For PIM, give the order, tone spacing, power per carrier and port definition. For out-of-band rejection, give the frequency range and attenuation target for each band that must be blocked. Low-PIM and rejection fields are only meaningful with those conditions attached. Computer-aided tuning of RF filters. Tuning practice is shown to explain parameter context, not to publish a product rating. RF specification fields to complete in the RFQ; target values remain project-specific. Parameter Target value Unit Test condition Required or goal Notes Passband / frequency range TBD MHz or GHz Band edge definition Required List guard bands and adjacent bands Bandwidth TBD MHz or % At stated return loss Required Note edge steepness or group delay Insertion loss TBD dB Over the full band Required State maximum or typical Return loss / VSWR TBD dB or ratio Reference impedance Required Per port where they differ Out-of-band rejection TBD dB Per stopband range Required One row per blocked band Port isolation TBD dB Defined port pair Required for multi-port parts State worst-case port Power handling TBD W or dBm CW or peak, duration Required Give power per port PIM TBD dBc Order, tones, power Where applicable Two-carrier test conditions Impedance TBD ohm Reference plane Required Usually 50 ohm; confirm if not Connectors and interfaces TBD Type Mating interface Required Flange, sex, torque or adapter Before you submit: check that each unit and test condition is present. Compare topology options on the RF filter product line or the combiner and duplexer product line before fixing mandatory targets. Background on topology and band planning is collected in engineering insights . Band Plan, Waveguide and Mechanical Inputs Combiners, waveguide assemblies and machined enclosures need different fields. FAQ RF Engineering Guide FAQs Which RF engineering guide should I read first? Choose by task rather than publication date. Start with a selection guide when topology is uncertain, a test-report guide when reviewing evidence, or the RFQ guide when specifications are mostly ready. Each article should provide comparison criteria, measurement conditions and a link to the relevant product family. What is the difference between a duplexer and a diplexer? A duplexer separates transmit and receive paths so they can share an antenna or port. A diplexer separates or combines different frequency bands. The suitable architecture depends on band plan, port definitions, isolation, insertion loss and power. Use the comparison guide, then submit the band plan through the combiner pathway. How should a low PIM design guide support product selection? It should connect PIM targets to frequency, power, connector, material, surface and test conditions rather than present a universal rating. Readers should record the applicable configuration and request supporting PIM evidence. Low PIM performance must be assessed for the specific model and conditions, not generalized across all products. What should I look for in an RF test report guide? Look for explanations of test setup, calibration, frequency range, acceptance limits and sample or lot identification. VNA curves, PIM results, reliability tests and matrix-switch automation answer different questions. Coverage must be defined for the applicable product and metric; a sample report shows evidence format, not a universal result. Can an engineering guide replace a custom RFQ review? No. A guide helps define topology, specifications and evidence needs, but feasibility still depends on the actual band plan, mechanical envelope, environment and validation requirements. Submit those inputs for review. A complete RFQ can receive initial engineering feedback in about 24 hours, not an automatic quotation or lead-time commitment. Have a specification or drawing? pages.text_excerpt: Home Privacy Policy Legal · Personal information Privacy Policy This policy explains what information the SONNE website collects, why it is collected, how it is handled and what choices you have. It covers this website and the contact and RFQ forms on it. It does not replace project-specific confidentiality arrangements agreed in writing for a particular engagement. Effective date: 25 October 2026 On this page Scope and operator Information you provide Information collected automatically How information is used and shared Uploaded files and confidentiality Cookies and third-party links Retention and security Your rights, changes and contact Scope and Operator This policy applies to the SONNE website published at rf-sonne.com and to the information you send through its forms, email addresses and download links. In this policy, SONNE refers to the operator of this website, based in Cixi, Ningbo, Zhejiang, China. The website is intended for business and technical audiences evaluating RF and microwave components, waveguide assemblies, combiners, base-station RF products and precision enclosures. It is not directed to children, and we do not knowingly collect personal information from children. Information You Provide When you contact us or submit a request, you choose what to send. The forms on this site may ask for: identification and contact details, such as your name, company, work email address and telephone number; project context, such as country, product line, application, project stage, quantities, expected volume and target date; technical requirements, such as frequency range, band plan, interface, performance targets and enclosure dimensions; the content of your message, including notes about confidentiality; and files you upload, such as specifications, drawings, band plans or test requirements. You may also contact us directly by email. Please do not submit personal information about another person unless you are authorised to do so, and avoid sending sensitive personal information that is not needed for your inquiry. Information Collected Automatically Like most websites, this site is served through hosting infrastructure that may record standard request information. This can include your IP address, browser type and version, device information, the page requested, the referring address and the time of the request. These records are used to deliver the site, maintain security, diagnose faults and understand aggregate traffic levels. The public pages of this website do not currently include advertising or behavioural analytics scripts. If this changes, this policy will be updated before those tools are introduced. How Information Is Used and Shared We use the information you provide to: respond to your question and confirm what you need; review a technical requirement and prepare engineering feedback or a quotation; discuss specifications, drawings, quantities and next steps with you; maintain business records and follow up on an active project; and protect the website, prevent misuse and comply with applicable legal obligations. Information may be seen by SONNE staff who need it for these purposes. We may also use service providers that support the website, hosting, email delivery, security or document storage. They receive only the access needed to provide those services and are expected to protect the information they handle. We do not sell personal information. We may disclose information where required by law, to respond to a valid legal request, to protect our rights or the safety of others, or as part of a corporate transaction subject to appropriate safeguards. SONNE is based in China. Information may be processed in China and in other countries where our service providers operate. Where applicable law requires safeguards for an international transfer, we take steps to apply them. Uploaded Files and Confidentiality Files submitted through the RFQ form are stored privately and are not published on the website. They are made available to SONNE staff who need them to review your requirement. Choosing the confidentiality option tells us that confidentiality should be discussed before sensitive material is exchanged. It does not by itself create a confidentiality agreement. If your files are sensitive, describe the requirement first and wait until a project-specific arrangement has been confirmed by both parties before uploading detailed material. Cookies and Third-Party Links The public pages of this site do not require an account and do not set advertising cookies. If you sign in to the administration area, WordPress may set functional cookies for authentication and display preferences. These cookies support the login session and are not used for advertising. The site may link to third-party websites, for example a map, documentation page or industry resource. Those sites operate under their own privacy policies, and we are not responsible for their content or practices. Following an external link is at your own discretion. Retention and Security We keep inquiry and project records for as long as needed to respond, maintain the business relationship, meet legal, accounting or security requirements, and resolve disputes. When information is no longer needed for these purposes, we delete it or remove the elements that identify you. We use reasonable technical and organisational measures to protect information against unauthorised access, loss or misuse. No website, email system or storage method is completely secure, so please avoid sending sensitive material by email unless it is necessary for your inquiry. Your Rights, Changes and Contact Where applicable law provides these rights, you may ask to access the personal information we hold about you, correct it, delete it, restrict or object to its use, or receive a portable copy. You may also withdraw consent where processing is based on consent. These rights are not absolute, and we may need to keep certain records for legal or security reasons. To make a request, email info@zhide-tec.com with the subject line “Privacy request” and enough detail for us to identify the relevant inquiry. We may ask you to verify your identity before acting on a request, and we will respond within a reasonable period. We may update this policy as the website or our practices change. The effective date at the top of this page shows the current version, and material changes will be reflected here. Privacy questions and requests: info@zhide-tec.com Telephone: +86-0574-63615958 SONNE No. 87, 89, 91, Sanbei Middle Road, Xinze Village, Guanhaiwei Town, Cixi City, Ningbo City, Zhejiang Province, China For a project-specific question, use the contact form or read the RFQ guide before submitting a request.

pages.text_excerpt: Home Resources Insights Low PIM & Combiners RF Diplexer: Band Routing, Isolation and Selection Low PIM & Combiners RF Diplexer: Band Routing, Isolation and Selection Oct 28, 2026 7 min read SONNE Engineering On this page What an RF Diplexer Does Diplexer Configurations in Practice Cavity and Waveguide Diplexers Parameters That Decide Diplexer Performance Reading the Guard Band Requirement Power and PIM in Diplexer Applications Diplexer RFQ Checklist Frequently Asked Questions What is the difference between a diplexer and a duplexer? Can a diplexer combine two transmitters? How much isolation does a diplexer need? Can a diplexer feed a dual-band antenna with one connector? Conclusion An RF diplexer routes two frequency bands between a common port and two band ports. On a block diagram it looks like a splitter, but most of these projects run into three inputs that were never stated: the guard band between the passbands, the match at the common port, and the power each band actually carries. This guide explains how the device works, which parameters decide its performance, and what an RFQ needs so that the quoted part matches the system rather than the product name. What an RF Diplexer Does A diplexer separates or combines two different frequency bands. Each band port passes its own band and rejects the other, and the common port connects to the antenna, feeder or distribution path. The device is reciprocal, so the same hardware splits one feed into two bands or combines two bands into one feed. The requirement is band-based, not direction-based. Each band port may carry a transmit signal, a receive signal, or both in a time-division system. That is what separates a diplexer from a duplexer, which separates transmit and receive directions of the same radio. When the architecture is still open, the duplexer vs diplexer comparison sets out the decision; this guide assumes the band-based case and focuses on specifying the part. A multiplexer extends the same principle to three or more bands. Every additional band adds another junction interaction, so the common-port match and the isolation between non-adjacent bands both become harder to hold. Diplexer Configurations in Practice The most common configuration is a dual-band antenna fed by one cable: two radios connect to the band ports, the antenna connects to the common port, and each radio sees only its own band. A second configuration combines two sub-bands of the same direction into one broadband path, for example when a radio covers two transmit sub-bands that must share a feeder. Diplexers also appear in distributed antenna systems, where several bands are combined into one distribution path and must remain isolated from each other. The IBS and DAS component line covers that context. In every configuration the internal structure is the same: two band-selective filter paths meeting at a common junction. The filters set the passbands and the rejection; the junction sets the common-port match and how the two paths interact. Representative two-way multi-band combiner hardware. A diplexer is the two-band case; the internal filters and the common-port junction decide isolation and loss, so the datasheet conditions matter more than the package photo. Cavity and Waveguide Diplexers The electrical function is the same, but the realization changes with frequency, power and size. Cavity diplexers are common at lower bands where the enclosure can be compact and the filters can be tuned after assembly. Waveguide diplexers are used at higher frequencies and in applications where low loss and high power handling matter; the flange interface and the machining tolerance then become part of the electrical specification. The waveguide component line covers diplexers built in waveguide, including the flange and assembly details that decide repeatability. In both realizations, the tolerance chain from machining to plating to tuning determines whether the guard band and isolation hold across a production run, not only on the first article. Parameters That Decide Diplexer Performance Six parameters carry most of the risk. Each one needs a value, a frequency reference and a test condition; a diplexer datasheet that quotes a single typical number without them cannot be compared with another supplier’s. Parameter What it controls What to state Passbands and guard band Which frequencies pass and how close the two bands sit Lower and upper band edges per port; the separation between them Insertion loss Signal loss through each band path Loss per band, across the band, with connectors included or excluded Band-to-band isolation How much signal from one band reaches the other port Isolation across each band, with the remaining ports terminated Common-port return loss Match seen by the antenna or feeder Return loss across both bands at the common port Power handling What each band port can carry, and whether both transmit at once Average and peak power per band; simultaneous or exclusive PIM Intermodulation produced in the filters and the common junction Carrier frequencies, power per carrier, order and measurement frequency Reading the Guard Band Requirement The guard band is the frequency space between the two passbands. A wide guard band allows simpler filters, lower loss and a more compact layout. A narrow guard band forces higher-order filtering, more resonators and tighter manufacturing control, and the insertion loss rises as a result. Rejection should be specified where it matters: inside the other band’s passband, not only at the band edge. A diplexer can show strong rejection at the crossover and still leak at the far end of the adjacent band if the filter skirt is not defined there. State the rejection mask across the full band to be protected, and state the termination used for the measurement. Power and PIM in Diplexer Applications Unlike a duplexer, a diplexer may have power on both band ports at the same time. If both bands transmit simultaneously, the common junction carries the sum, and the filters must handle their own band without arcing, heating or drifting. That condition belongs in the RFQ; a rating quoted for one band alone does not cover it. PIM is generated where current density and material interfaces are least controlled: connector joints, tuning elements, plating transitions and the common junction. Specify the two carrier frequencies, the power per carrier, the intermodulation order and the measurement frequency. A low-power or single-carrier test does not predict multi-carrier behavior, so the PIM requirement should be tied to the actual configuration. The testing and quality process describes how VNA and PIM evidence is produced and recorded. Diplexer RFQ Checklist Band edges for each port, and the guard band between them. Rejection mask inside the opposite band, with the termination used for the test. Insertion loss and return loss per band, and the common-port return loss across both bands. Power per band, average and peak, and whether both bands transmit simultaneously. PIM order, carrier frequencies, power per carrier and measurement frequency. Connector or flange types, port orientation, mounting and the available envelope. Test evidence and acceptance limits for the first article and for production lots. These inputs let the supplier choose the filter order and the junction design against the real requirement instead of quoting a catalogue part. They also make two quotations comparable, because each number carries the same condition. Frequently Asked Questions What is the difference between a diplexer and a duplexer? A diplexer separates two frequency bands, while a duplexer separates transmit and receive directions of one radio. Both can share a common antenna port, but the isolation requirements and the port map differ. The comparison guide covers the decision in detail. Can a diplexer combine two transmitters? Filter Selection Cavity vs Waveguide Filter Selection: Which Topology Fits Your RF Design? Oct 26, 2026 7 min read SONNE Engineering On this page Two Topologies, Two Loss Mechanisms Cavity vs Waveguide Filter Comparison at a Glance Frequency and Bandwidth Come First Insertion Loss and Rejection Trade-Offs Power Handling and PIM Size, Weight and Integration Tuning, Repeatability and Volume Cavity vs Waveguide Filter Selection Checklist Frequently Asked Questions Is a waveguide filter always lower loss than a cavity filter? Which topology is better for low PIM? Can a cavity filter be used at E-band? The cavity vs waveguide filter decision starts with the same frequency-selection problem, but the two topologies use different loss mechanisms, power limits and manufacturing constraints, so the right choice depends on where the filter sits in the system rather than on a single performance number. Two Topologies, Two Loss Mechanisms A cavity filter uses resonant structures machined into a metal housing, with coupling between resonators set by the mechanical layout. Energy is stored in the cavity fields and coupled through irises, probes or loops. The design is compact at lower frequencies and can be tuned after assembly, which makes it a practical choice for base-station, RRU and multi-band front-end products. A waveguide filter uses a section of waveguide with resonant cavities or corrugations. At high frequencies the waveguide itself has low loss, and the filter can handle high power because the fields are distributed in a larger metal structure. The trade-off is size: a waveguide filter for a low-frequency band can be physically large, while the same topology at E-band becomes compact enough for an outdoor radio. Cavity vs Waveguide Filter Comparison at a Glance Selection factor Cavity filter Waveguide filter Typical role Base-station, RRU, compact front ends Backhaul, satellite, radar, high-frequency links Insertion loss Moderate; depends on resonator count and tuning Low at high frequency; depends on length and surface quality Rejection Good with multiple resonators; layout constrained by size Strong in a compact high-frequency package Power handling Limited by tuning elements, contacts and connectors High when the waveguide and flange are sized correctly Size and mass Compact at lower bands Large at lower bands; compact at E-band and above Manufacturing route CNC housing, assembly, tuning, test Precision machining, split-block assembly, plating, test Tuning Tunable after assembly; useful for prototypes Often fixed by machining; tuning is limited or avoided Best fit Flexible electrical requirements and volume production High frequency, low loss, high power and stable repeatability Frequency and Bandwidth Come First Start with the passband and the fractional bandwidth. A narrowband filter with a high rejection requirement tends to need more resonators, which increases insertion loss and manufacturing sensitivity. A wideband requirement can be difficult for a cavity design because the coupling values and the physical layout become harder to realize, while a waveguide structure may handle the bandwidth more naturally at high frequency. The operating frequency also changes the practical size. Below a few gigahertz, a cavity filter usually fits the available radio envelope and a waveguide filter may be too large. At E-band and above, the waveguide wavelength is small enough that a precision machined filter can be both compact and low loss. The frequency range is therefore not a marketing detail; it is the first constraint that decides which topology deserves detailed evaluation. Insertion Loss and Rejection Trade-Offs Insertion loss is set by the number of resonators, the quality factor of the structure, the surface condition and the interface losses. A higher-order filter can improve rejection, but each additional resonator adds loss and narrows the manufacturing window. The right question is not “what is the lowest loss” but “what loss can the system budget tolerate while still meeting the rejection mask”. Rejection should be evaluated at specific frequency offsets. A filter with excellent rejection far from the passband may have inadequate rejection at the first adjacent channel, and vice versa. For a receive path, the critical case is often the transmitter band or the image frequency; for a transmit path, it may be the harmonic or the receive band. State the rejection mask and the measurement range so the topology comparison uses the same criteria. Return loss also belongs in the comparison. A filter that meets its amplitude response but presents a poor match can degrade the performance of the amplifier or antenna behind it. Cavity and waveguide designs have different matching behavior over bandwidth, so the interface should be evaluated together with the filter response. Power Handling and PIM Waveguide filters generally handle more power because the fields are distributed across a larger metal surface and there are fewer lossy joints in the main path. Cavity filters can also handle significant power, but the tuning screws, internal contacts, connector interfaces and plating quality become limiting factors. The waveform matters: a continuous carrier, a pulsed signal and a multi-carrier signal impose different stresses. For low-PIM applications, the entire current path matters. Connector torque, plating, joint pressure, material choice and cleanliness can dominate the result. A cavity design with many tuning elements has more interfaces to control, while a waveguide design with a split block has fewer but highly critical seams. Neither topology is automatically low PIM; both require a defined assembly and test process. PIM should be specified with carrier frequencies, power per carrier and intermodulation order so the result can be compared. Representative waveguide hardware. Filter assemblies depend on the same flange accuracy, surface finish and machining discipline as the waveguide run around them. Size, Weight and Integration Mechanical fit often decides the topology before the electrical comparison is complete. A cavity filter can be integrated into a radio housing with a compact footprint, but it needs access for tuning and may require a specific mounting orientation. A waveguide filter needs straight runs, flange access and enough space for the assembly and test fixtures. At E-band, the waveguide filter may be smaller than the cavity alternative, but the flange and split-block tolerances become more demanding. Include the available envelope, mounting points, connector or flange orientation and service access in the evaluation. A design that meets the electrical target but cannot be assembled or tuned in the intended enclosure is not a valid selection. Tuning, Repeatability and Volume A tunable cavity filter is useful during development because the response can be adjusted after assembly. For mass production, the same tuning step must be controlled and verified so that unit-to-unit variation stays inside the specification. A tuning-free design can remove that step, but it shifts the burden to machining accuracy, material consistency and assembly control. Waveguide filters are often designed as fixed tuned parts. That suits repeatable production when the machining and plating processes are stable, but it leaves less room for correcting a design error after the parts are made. The prototype and first-article stages should therefore include a measured comparison against the simulation and a clear plan for any required adjustment. Cavity vs Waveguide Filter Selection Checklist State the passband, bandwidth and rejection mask before comparing topologies. Check whether the available envelope favors a compact cavity or a low-loss waveguide structure. Confirm the power waveform, average power and peak power. Define PIM order, carrier power

Can I submit a partial RFQ? Does an RFQ create a binding quotation? A custom RF filter quote is only as good as the inputs behind it, so an RF filter RFQ should describe the signal path, the electrical limits and the mechanical envelope in one reviewable package. Why RF Filter RFQs Stall at the First Review Most delayed filter projects do not fail because the specification is difficult. They stall because the first RFQ leaves engineering to guess. A request that says “bandpass filter at 2.6 GHz” without a bandwidth, a rejection mask or a power condition cannot be evaluated as a design. The supplier must either ask for clarification or quote a generic catalogue part that may not fit the application. A reviewable RFQ does not need to be a formal document. It needs to answer three questions in order: what signal must pass, what signal must be rejected, and what space and environment the hardware must survive. When those answers are present, an engineer can identify the likely topology, the critical manufacturing features and the test method before any quotation work begins. Start With the Band Plan and Signal Path The band plan is the foundation of filter selection. State the passband edges, not only the center frequency, and identify the transmit and receive paths if both are present. If the filter sits in a duplexer, combiner or multi-band front end, include the other bands and the duplex spacing. A filter that looks straightforward in isolation can become difficult when a nearby blocking signal sits close to the passband edge. Also describe the system role in one sentence. A receive filter protecting a low-noise amplifier has different priorities from a transmit filter handling high power, and a filter used in a test bench may need a different connector and tuning approach from one sealed inside an outdoor radio unit. RFQ input What to state Why engineering needs it Passband Lower and upper frequency, center frequency, bandwidth Sets resonator count and coupling topology Signal path Tx, Rx, common port, or bidirectional Determines power, isolation and port definition Nearby bands Co-sited transmitters, duplex spacing, guard bands Defines the rejection mask and isolation target Reference hardware Existing part number, curve or drawing Shortens the path to a comparable design Specify Insertion Loss, Return Loss and Rejection as Numbers Insertion loss should be stated as a maximum over the passband, with the temperature range and the measurement conditions that apply. If the system budget assumes a typical value, say so and state the maximum the system can tolerate. “Low loss” is not a specification because it cannot be verified. Return loss, or VSWR, belongs in the RFQ for the same reason. A filter can meet its passband shape while presenting a poor match at one port, which then interacts with the cable or amplifier behind it. State the required return loss across the passband and whether it applies at every port. Rejection is most useful as a mask: a table of frequency ranges and minimum attenuation. For example, a receive filter may need one rejection level at the transmitter band, a different level at the image frequency and a third level across a broadband measurement range. A single rejection number hides these requirements and makes the design appear easier or harder than it is. For multi-port parts, define isolation between ports in the same way. State whether isolation is measured with the other ports terminated and whether it must hold across temperature. Add Power, PIM and Environmental Conditions Power handling depends on the waveform, not only on a single watt figure. State average power, peak power, modulation, duty cycle and the expected load mismatch. A filter rated for a continuous carrier may behave differently with a pulsed or multi-carrier signal, and the tuning elements, connectors and internal contacts all contribute to the limit. Passive intermodulation, or PIM, must be tied to a test condition. Specify the two carrier frequencies, the power per carrier, the intermodulation order and the frequency at which the product is measured. A PIM target without those conditions cannot be compared between suppliers. Material selection, plating, joint design and connector torque all affect the result, so PIM should be treated as a configuration-specific requirement rather than a universal rating. Environmental inputs complete the electrical picture: operating and storage temperature, humidity, ingress protection, corrosion exposure, altitude, vibration and any applicable test standard. If a specific acceptance test is required, name it. If the filter will be sealed or potted, say so because the assembly and test sequence may change. Define Connectors, Flanges and the Mechanical Envelope The mechanical section should include connector or flange type, gender, torque requirement and port orientation. For coaxial parts, state whether the connector is standard or custom and whether a specific cable interface must be matched. For waveguide parts, state the waveguide size, flange standard and whether a straight, right-angle or split-block assembly is expected. Provide a 2D drawing or a 3D model with the mounting points, keep-out zones, cable routing and maximum mass. If no drawing exists, a dimensioned sketch with the available volume is enough to start. The most common mechanical problem is not a tight tolerance; it is a filter that meets the electrical target but cannot be installed, tuned or serviced in the intended enclosure. Representative multi-cavity filter hardware. The RFQ should define the passband, rejection mask, power condition and mechanical envelope before tuning begins. State Prototype and Volume Intent Tell the supplier where the project is in its lifecycle: engineering prototype, design verification, pilot run or mass production. Include the quantity for each stage and the target dates that matter. This helps engineering choose a tuning strategy, a test plan and a manufacturing route that can survive the transition to volume. If the project requires a first article inspection report, a VNA data file, a PIM report or a specific traceability format, include that requirement in the RFQ. These deliverables affect the test flow and should be agreed before the first hardware is built rather than after it is measured. A Reviewable RF Filter RFQ Package A complete package can be assembled from the following items. Not every project needs every line, but each missing line should be a conscious decision rather than an oversight. One-sentence description of the system, the filter function and the signal path. Band plan table with passband edges, center frequency and bandwidth. Rejection or isolation mask by frequency range. Maximum insertion loss and minimum return loss over temperature. Average power, peak power, waveform and load condition. PIM order, carrier power and measurement frequencies, if applicable. Connector or flange definition, port orientation and torque. 2D drawing or 3D model with mounting and keep-out dimensions. Environmental conditions and any required acceptance tests. Which isolation value should I specify? Can a diplexer be used for low PIM applications? The duplexer vs diplexer decision is often treated as a naming question, but the architecture that fits a project depends on whether the ports carry different directions, different bands, or both, and that distinction changes the isolation, power and PIM requirements. Definitions That Survive a Procurement Review A duplexer separates the transmit and receive paths of a radio so that both can share one antenna or feeder. The two channel ports carry signals in opposite directions, and the common port connects to the antenna. The key requirement is usually duplex spacing: the frequency separation between the transmit and receive bands. The duplexer must pass each band with low loss while rejecting the other band strongly enough to protect the receiver and keep the transmitter energy out of the receive path. A diplexer separates or combines two different frequency bands, regardless of direction. It may combine two transmit bands, two receive bands, or a transmit band and a receive band into a common port. Its job is band-based routing: each channel port passes its own band and rejects the other. A multiplexer extends the same idea to three or more bands. In practice the physical hardware can look similar, and some products are described with both terms. The useful distinction is functional. Ask which ports carry which signal, what must be isolated from what, and whether the requirement is direction-based or band-based. Duplexer Architecture A duplexer normally contains two filter paths that meet at a common junction. The transmit filter must handle the transmit power and keep the transmit band clean; the receive filter must protect the receiver from the transmit signal and from nearby blockers. The common junction and the antenna interface are critical because any mismatch there affects both paths. Cavity duplexers are common in base-station and RRU products where the bands are relatively low and the mechanical envelope is tight. Waveguide duplexers are used at higher frequencies and in applications where low loss and high power handling matter. In both cases, the duplex spacing sets the difficulty: a narrow spacing requires sharper filters, more resonators and tighter manufacturing control. The transmit path also drives the PIM requirement. Two or more carriers in the transmit signal can mix at a nonlinear junction and produce intermodulation products that fall into the receive band. The duplexer must therefore be designed and assembled with a controlled current path, clean interfaces and a defined test condition. Diplexer Architecture A diplexer uses two band-selective paths that meet at a common port. Unlike a duplexer, the two paths may carry the same direction. A typical use is a dual-band antenna that must serve two radios or two sub-bands without a second feeder. The diplexer isolates the bands from each other and presents a controlled match at the common port. Because the requirement is band separation, the guard band between the two passbands is the critical parameter. A wide guard band allows simpler filters and a more compact layout. A narrow guard band demands higher-order filtering and tighter control of the manufacturing tolerances. If the two bands are close and the power is high, the diplexer can be as demanding as a duplexer even though the signal directions are the same. Duplexer vs Diplexer Comparison at a Glance Requirement Duplexer Diplexer Primary function Separate transmit and receive paths Separate or combine different bands Port signals Tx, Rx and common antenna Band A, band B and common port Critical spacing Duplex spacing between Tx and Rx Guard band between the two bands Isolation target Tx leakage into Rx; Rx protection Band-to-band isolation Power concern Transmit path and common junction Depends on which bands carry power PIM concern High when multiple Tx carriers share the path High when a high-power band is combined Typical use Base stations, RRUs, repeaters Dual-band antennas, multi-band front ends Isolation, Insertion Loss and Return Loss Isolation is not a single number that can be applied to every port. For a duplexer, the most important isolation path is usually from the transmit port to the receive port, measured across the receive band. For a diplexer, isolation is measured between the two channel ports across each band. In both cases, state the termination, the frequency range and the temperature condition. Insertion loss must be specified for each path separately. A duplexer may have a higher-loss transmit path because it needs more rejection, while the receive path is optimized for loss. A diplexer may have asymmetric losses if one band requires a sharper filter. A single “typical insertion loss” figure can hide the path that matters most. Return loss at the common port is equally important. The common port sees the antenna or feeder, and a poor match there can degrade both paths. Specify the return loss across the full operating band rather than at the centre frequency alone. Power and PIM Conditions For a duplexer, state the transmit power waveform, the average and peak power, and the expected load mismatch. The receive path may carry little power, but it must survive the transmit leakage that the duplexer itself does not absorb. For a diplexer, state which bands carry high power and whether both bands can transmit at the same time. PIM should be specified with two carrier frequencies, the power per carrier, the intermodulation order and the measurement frequency. A result measured at low power or with a single carrier does not predict performance in a multi-carrier system. The materials, plating, connector torque and joint design all contribute, so the PIM requirement should be tied to the actual configuration. Representative multi-band combiner hardware. A diplexer is the two-band case; adding bands increases the interaction between filters and the importance of the common-port match. Port Layout and Mechanical Integration The port arrangement often decides which architecture is practical. A duplexer needs a transmit port, a receive port and a common port, and the connector or flange orientation must suit the radio and the antenna feeder. A diplexer needs two band ports and a common port, and the two band ports may need to face different equipment. If the available envelope cannot accommodate the required port directions, a different package or a short jumper may be needed. Mounting, service access and cable routing belong in the RFQ. A combiner that meets the electrical specification but cannot be installed or serviced is a schedule risk. Include the mounting plane, the torque access, the maximum mass and any keep-out zones in the mechanical input. Duplexer vs Diplexer Selection Checklist Identify whether the requirement is direction-based (duplexer) or band-based (diplexer). State the duplex spacing or guard band and the rejection mask. Specify isolation, insertion loss and return loss per path and per port. Define the power waveform for each band and the load condition. State the PIM order, carrier power and measurement frequencies. Confirm the connector or flange layout and the available envelope. What to Specify in a Power Divider RFQ Frequently Asked Questions What is the difference between a Wilkinson and a reactive power divider? Can a Wilkinson power divider be used as a combiner? Does the isolation resistor limit power handling? How is power divider bandwidth defined? Conclusion A Wilkinson power divider is often selected by name alone, yet the name only tells you the topology. Whether the part suits a system depends on the isolation it provides, the bandwidth over which the ports stay matched, and what happens when one output is mismatched. This guide explains how the network works, how it compares with reactive and resistive dividers, and which values to put in an RFQ so that a supplier can quote the right device instead of a generic splitter. What Is a Wilkinson Power Divider? A Wilkinson power divider splits one input into two outputs of equal amplitude and phase while keeping all three ports matched and providing isolation between the outputs. It uses quarter-wave transmission-line sections and an isolation resistor between the output ports. The resistor carries no current when the outputs are matched and absorbs difference-mode power when they are not. The equal-split, 50 Ω case is the one most engineers meet first: each quarter-wave section has an impedance of about 70.7 Ω, and a 100 Ω resistor bridges the outputs. Unequal split ratios are possible by changing the line impedances and the resistor value, but the principle stays the same: the network trades bandwidth and physical size for match and isolation. How the Wilkinson Power Divider Works At the design frequency, a signal entering the input port divides equally. Because the two paths are identical, the outputs are in phase and at the same amplitude. The quarter-wave sections transform the load impedances so that the input sees the system impedance. Isolation comes from symmetry. When a signal is injected into one output while the other ports are terminated, the two paths present equal magnitudes with opposite phase at the resistor, so the difference appears across it and is dissipated. In the matched, equal-split case, the resistor sees no voltage and the divider behaves as a lossless network. That is why the topology is described as lossless in theory and why its excess loss in practice is set by conductor, dielectric and connector losses. Bandwidth is the main limitation. A single-section design operates over a moderate band; multi-section designs add quarter-wave sections and resistors to widen the band at the cost of length and complexity. An N-way Wilkinson uses several sections and resistors, and its isolation is defined between specific output ports, so the port map must be stated clearly. Representative two-way power splitter hardware. A product photo does not confirm the internal topology; ask for the topology, isolation data and test conditions for the specified band. Wilkinson vs Reactive vs Resistive Power Dividers Three topologies cover most power-divider requirements. They are not interchangeable, and the choice usually comes down to whether output isolation or low loss matters more. Property Wilkinson Reactive Resistive Output isolation Provided by the isolation resistor Limited; no isolation resistor Limited Excess loss Low when matched; mismatch power dissipates in the resistor Low; no resistor loss, mismatch is reflected Fixed and highest Bandwidth Moderate for one section; wider with multiple sections Usually narrower; depends on network order Broadband Power handling Set by the resistor, connectors and thermal design Set by conductors and dielectrics; no resistor to burn out Set by resistor rating and heating Typical use Antenna feeds, test paths and systems needing matched, isolated outputs Low-loss combining or splitting where efficiency dominates Broadband monitoring and low-cost splitting A reactive divider uses an L-C or transmission-line network without a lossy resistor. It can be very efficient and robust, but it does not isolate the outputs, so a mismatch on one port affects the other. A resistive divider is simple and broadband, but its loss is fixed and it does not replace a low-loss design. For low-PIM splitters and couplers used in indoor DAS, the topology and materials are chosen around the PIM requirement rather than the divider name; the IBS and DAS component line covers that context. Reading a Power Divider Datasheet Datasheets mix theoretical split loss with measured insertion loss, and that is where most comparisons go wrong. Split loss is not insertion loss An ideal two-way divider delivers half the power to each output, which is 3.01 dB below the input. A three-way divider delivers 4.77 dB per output, and a four-way divider 6.02 dB. These figures are split loss, not loss in the component. Insertion loss is the additional loss above the split ratio; when a datasheet quotes “insertion loss” without stating whether split loss is included, ask for the definition. Isolation and return loss measure different things Isolation is measured between output ports with the remaining ports terminated, and it describes how much signal reaches the other output. Return loss describes how well each port matches its termination. A part can have good return loss and modest isolation, or the reverse. Specify both, and state the frequency range and termination used for the measurement. Amplitude and phase balance For a two-way divider, amplitude balance is the difference in output power and phase balance is the difference in output phase. Both matter for antenna arrays and for combining, where imbalance turns into reflected power and heat. Specify balance across the band, not at the centre frequency alone. Power handling and derating The forward power rating is only the starting point. The isolation resistor must survive mismatch, phase error and temperature, and in a combining application the dissipated power can rise sharply. State the load VSWR, the expected phase and amplitude spread, the ambient temperature and the duty cycle so that the supplier can check the thermal design. Power Divider or Combiner? The same network works in both directions. Used as a divider, one input feeds two outputs. Used as a combiner, two inputs feed one output. The difference is the signal relationship: two coherent, well-matched signals combine efficiently, while uncorrelated signals or phase errors produce mismatch power that the isolation resistor must absorb. That is why a part rated for splitting may not be suitable for combining at the same power. If the application combines different frequency bands rather than the same band, a frequency-selective combiner or duplexer is the right device; the RF combiner and duplexer line explains the difference, and the duplexer vs diplexer guide covers the band-based case. Amplitude and phase balance limits, measured across the band. Power: forward power, load VSWR, phase and amplitude spread, ambient temperature and duty cycle.
