pages.text_excerpt: Home Resources Insights Waveguide & E-Band E-Band Waveguide Diplexer Design: Flange, Tolerance and Test Requirements Waveguide & E-Band E-Band Waveguide Diplexer Design: Flange, Tolerance and Test Requirements Oct 25, 2026 7 min read SONNE Engineering On this page What an E-Band Diplexer Does Start With the Band Plan and Port Definition Flange and Waveguide Interface Machining Tolerance and Split-Block Design Plating, Assembly and Cleanliness Isolation, Return Loss and Power VNA Verification and Test Setup RFQ Inputs for an E-Band Diplexer Frequently Asked Questions Which waveguide and flange are used at E-band? Why is split-block machining critical for an E-band diplexer? Can an E-band diplexer be tuned after assembly? An E-band waveguide diplexer combines two millimetre-wave channels onto a shared antenna port, and its performance is decided as much by flange accuracy, split-block machining and assembly discipline as by the filter design itself. What an E-Band Diplexer Does E-band links commonly use the 71–76 GHz and 81–86 GHz allocations. A diplexer separates or combines these channels so that a single antenna can serve both directions or both sub-bands while keeping the transmit and receive paths isolated. The part is a passive waveguide assembly with two channel ports and one common port, and its response must hold across the full operating band, not only at the centre frequency. At these frequencies the waveguide wavelength is short, so every mechanical feature is electrically significant. A small step at a flange joint, a burr inside a channel or a plating thickness variation can change the return loss and the isolation. The E-band waveguide diplexer therefore needs to be evaluated as a manufactured assembly, not only as an electromagnetic model. Start With the Band Plan and Port Definition Define the two channel bands, the common port, the polarization and the direction of each signal path. State whether the diplexer is used for transmit and receive separation, for two sub-bands in the same radio, or for combining two outdoor units onto one antenna. The port definition determines the isolation requirement and the power handling on each path. Also state the guard band between channels and the rejection required outside each passband. A diplexer with a narrow guard band demands sharper filters and tighter manufacturing control than one with a wide separation. If the radio uses a duplex spacing inside one of the channels, include that spacing because it affects the internal filter order and the isolation target. Flange and Waveguide Interface For E-band waveguide diplexer hardware, a common interface is WR-12 waveguide with UG-387/U flanges. The flange must be flat, correctly aligned and free of damage, because a poor joint adds reflection and can create a leakage path. Specify the flange type, the number and position of the alignment holes, the screw thread and the required torque. If the mating flange is a different standard, state the adapter or transition that will be used and who supplies it. Flange orientation is also a mechanical constraint. The assembly must be accessible with a torque tool, and the waveguide runs must not place stress on the joints. In an outdoor unit, the interface may need a gasket or a sealed transition; that requirement should be part of the RFQ because it can change the mechanical design and the test fixture. Surface finish at the flange face and inside the waveguide is part of the RF interface. Scratches, oxidation and plating defects increase loss and can cause PIM or leakage. Define the acceptable finish and the inspection method rather than relying on a visual check at assembly. Machining Tolerance and Split-Block Design E-band diplexers are often machined as split blocks: two or more metal pieces are aligned, clamped and joined so that the internal waveguide channels are formed by the mating surfaces. The alignment of those surfaces, the flatness of the split and the position of the internal features determine whether the assembled part matches the model. For high-frequency hardware, machining tolerance can reach ±0.01 mm and plating thickness can be controlled to about 1 μm on qualified designs. Those numbers are not a universal specification; they describe what is achievable when the geometry, material and process are selected for the requirement. The RFQ should state the critical dimensions and the allowed deviation, not only a general tolerance block. Corner radii, iris thickness, channel depth and the transition between waveguide sections all need to be manufacturable with the selected tooling. A design that is elegant in simulation but requires an inaccessible tool path will either be expensive or will be modified late in the project. A design-for-manufacturing review before the first cut is cheaper than re-machining a split block. Plating, Assembly and Cleanliness Silver or gold plating is commonly used to control surface conductivity and corrosion. The plating must be uniform inside the waveguide, free of voids and nodules, and thick enough to be stable through assembly and environmental exposure. Plating thickness and adhesion should be inspected on critical surfaces, not only on an external coupon. Assembly introduces the joints that the model does not show. Screw torque, joint pressure, alignment pins and the order of tightening all affect the electrical result. Cleanliness matters as well: metal particles, dust or plating flakes inside a millimetre-wave channel can create a local discontinuity or a breakdown path. A defined cleaning and inspection step belongs in the process, especially for high-power or low-PIM designs. Representative waveguide front-end hardware. E-band assemblies depend on precision flanges, split-block alignment and controlled plating as much as on the filter response. Isolation, Return Loss and Power Isolation between the channel ports is a primary diplexer requirement. State the minimum isolation across each passband and the conditions under which it is measured, including termination and temperature. Return loss at the common port and at each channel port must also be specified, because a diplexer that isolates well but presents a poor match can degrade the radio and the antenna system. Power handling depends on the signal, the pressure inside the waveguide and the loss at the joints. For transmit paths, state average power, peak power and waveform. For receive paths, the concern may be the leakage from the transmit channel rather than the absolute power. If the assembly will be used outdoors, include the environmental conditions and any pressurization or sealing requirement. VNA Verification and Test Setup Millimetre-wave measurements are only as good as the calibration and the fixture. A waveguide calibration kit, a stable test port and a repeatable connection procedure are essential. The test report should identify the calibration method, the reference plane, the frequency range, the number of points and the instrument settings. Without those details, a curve cannot be compared with another supplier’s data. For a diplexer, the test plan should cover transmission and reflection at every port, isolation between channel ports, and the common-port match. If PIM or high-power testing is required, it should be defined separately because the fixture and the environment are different. Temperature testing adds another variable: the mechanical assembly and the plated surfaces expand differently, so the response should be verified at the temperature extremes that the application requires. RFQ Inputs for an E-Band Diplexer Channel bands, guard band and common-port definition. Isolation and rejection mask for each path. Maximum insertion loss and minimum return loss at every port. Average power, peak power and waveform for each channel. Waveguide size, flange standard, orientation and mating hardware. Split-block or monolithic preference, material and plating. pages.text_excerpt: Home Resources Insights Test Reports & Verification How to Read an RF Test Report: VNA, PIM and Acceptance Limits Test Reports & Verification How to Read an RF Test Report: VNA, PIM and Acceptance Limits Oct 25, 2026 7 min read SONNE Engineering On this page A Test Report Is Evidence, Not a Brochure Identify the Device Under Test Read the VNA Setup and Calibration Interpret the S-Parameters and Limits Understand the PIM Test Conditions Review Reliability and Environmental Data Separately Traceability and Acceptance Red Flags in an RF Test Report Frequently Asked Questions What should an RF test report include at minimum? Can I compare reports from two suppliers directly? Does a passing report guarantee field performance? An RF test report is evidence that a specific piece of hardware met a defined limit under a defined measurement setup, and it should be read with the same care as the specification it is meant to prove. A Test Report Is Evidence, Not a Brochure A report that shows a smooth curve and a green “PASS” stamp is not enough. The reader needs to know what was measured, how it was measured, which unit was measured and what limit applied. Without that context, two reports cannot be compared, and a purchasing decision may rest on a curve that belongs to a different configuration or a different test condition. The first check is whether the report matches the part number, revision and configuration in the purchase order. A report for a connectorized prototype does not automatically apply to a sealed production unit, and a report measured with a different flange or cable interface may not represent the delivered hardware. Identify the Device Under Test Look for the part number, serial number or lot code, the hardware revision and the date of test. If the report covers a sample from a production lot, the sample identity and the sampling basis should be stated. If it covers a first article, the drawing revision and the approved configuration should be referenced. The configuration details matter: connector types, flange standards, cable lengths, adapters and any test fixture. A measurement that includes a long cable or an adapter is still valid, but the reference plane must be clear. Otherwise the insertion loss may include test hardware rather than the device alone. Read the VNA Setup and Calibration For S-parameter measurements, the report should identify the instrument, the calibration method, the calibration kit, the reference plane, the frequency range, the number of points and the intermediate frequency bandwidth. Averaging and smoothing should also be disclosed because they can make a noisy response look cleaner than it is. Calibration is the foundation of the measurement. A coaxial calibration may use short-open-load-through, while a waveguide measurement may use through-reflect-line. The method should suit the interface and the frequency range. If the report does not state the calibration method or the reference plane, the reader cannot tell whether a flange or connector effect has been removed. Measurement uncertainty is another useful indicator. A limit that sits inside the uncertainty band of the test setup is difficult to judge. A mature report states the uncertainty or at least the repeatability of the measurement so the reader knows how much margin the result represents. Interpret the S-Parameters and Limits Insertion loss is usually read from the transmission coefficient across the passband. Check whether the reported value is a maximum, a minimum or a typical, and whether it includes the test fixture. Return loss is read from the reflection coefficient; confirm whether the report shows return loss in decibels or VSWR, because the two are related but not interchangeable. Rejection and isolation should be read against the frequency mask, not only at a single point. A curve that meets the limit at the centre of the stopband may fail at the band edge. Look for the worst-case value inside each specified range and compare it with the limit that applies to that range. Also check the frequency range and the number of points. A narrow measurement range can miss a spurious response, and a coarse frequency grid can miss a narrow resonance. The report should cover the range that the specification defines, with enough resolution to support the acceptance decision. VNA-based alignment and verification. The test report should identify the setup, calibration and reference plane behind the curves, not only the final pass or fail result. Understand the PIM Test Conditions Passive intermodulation results are meaningless without the test conditions. The report should state the two carrier frequencies, the power per carrier, the intermodulation order, the measurement frequency and the test equipment. It should also state how the device was terminated and whether the test was performed in a controlled environment. A PIM value measured at low power cannot be extrapolated to a high-power site condition. The third-order product is the most common reported metric, but fifth-order and seventh-order products may matter in some systems. If the specification calls for a particular order and power, confirm that the report uses the same basis. PIM is sensitive to connector torque, cable movement, contamination and nearby metal. A report should identify the test configuration and any handling precautions. If the result is close to the limit, the repeatability of the setup becomes part of the evidence. Review Reliability and Environmental Data Separately VNA and PIM data describe RF performance at the time of test. Reliability and environmental tests answer a different question: whether the performance survives temperature cycling, humidity, corrosion, vibration or other exposures. Read those results against the applicable test standard and the duration or number of cycles. Check whether the RF performance was measured before and after the exposure, and whether the acceptance criteria are the same. A report that shows only a visual inspection after an environmental test does not demonstrate RF stability. A report that shows a full S-parameter comparison before and after is more useful, provided the test conditions and sample identity are clear. Traceability and Acceptance Traceability connects the report to the hardware. Look for a serial or lot number, the test date, the operator or station identifier and the instrument calibration status. If the report is issued for a production lot, the sampling plan and the treatment of nonconforming units should be defined. The acceptance section should state the specification, the measured result and the pass or fail decision for each parameter. A report that lists only measured values without limits leaves the reader to reconstruct the acceptance criteria. A report that lists only pass or fail without data cannot show how much margin exists. Red Flags in an RF Test Report No part number, revision or serial or lot identity. No calibration method, reference plane or instrument status. Limits that are not connected to a specification or drawing. Curves that are smoothed without disclosure. PIM results without carrier power, frequencies or intermodulation order. Environmental results without before-and-after RF measurements. Pass or fail statements with no measured data behind them. For a wider view of how SONNE handles VNA, PIM, reliability and matrix-switch testing, see testing and quality . The manufacturing page covers process control, and the RF and microwave filter product line shows the product context. If a project needs a specific report format or data package, state it in the RFQ and submit the requirement through Request a Quote . Frequently Asked Questions What should an RF test report include at minimum? Device identity, configuration, test date, instrument and calibration details, frequency range, measurement setup, acceptance limits, measured results and a clear pass or fail decision. pages.text_excerpt: Home Resources Insights NPI & Manufacturing RF NPI Guide: From Prototype and First Article to Pilot Run NPI & Manufacturing RF NPI Guide: From Prototype and First Article to Pilot Run Oct 25, 2026 7 min read SONNE Engineering On this page What RF NPI Means for Custom RF Hardware Requirements Review and Design for Manufacturability Prototype and Design Verification First Article Inspection Pilot Run and Process Capability Golden Sample and Test Baseline Change Control and Mass Production RF NPI Checklist Frequently Asked Questions What is the difference between a prototype and a first article? Why is a pilot run necessary if the prototype passed? What is a golden sample used for? An RF NPI process turns a working prototype into a production item that can be built, tested and shipped repeatedly, and the discipline that matters most is the evidence carried from one stage to the next. What RF NPI Means for Custom RF Hardware New product introduction, or NPI, is the controlled path from a specification to a production-ready product. For a custom RF filter, waveguide assembly, combiner or enclosure, the path includes design review, prototype build, measurement, first article approval, pilot production and the transition to volume. The exact stage names vary by company, but the purpose does not: reduce risk before the design is locked and before tooling or production capacity is committed. RF hardware adds a specific difficulty. The electrical response is sensitive to dimensions, material, plating, assembly pressure and test setup, so a design that works in simulation can still fail when it is machined and assembled. NPI is the process that closes that gap with measured evidence rather than assumption. Requirements Review and Design for Manufacturability The first stage is a structured review of the specification. The engineering team checks whether the electrical targets are self-consistent, whether the mechanical envelope allows the required topology, and whether the power, PIM, environmental and test requirements can be verified. Missing inputs are identified before the design is released rather than after the first parts are made. Design for manufacturability, or DFM, follows. The review looks at tolerances, tool access, surface finish, plating, assembly sequence and test access. A cavity filter may need tuning access that conflicts with a sealed enclosure; a waveguide diplexer may need a split-block joint that is difficult to align; an enclosure may need a bend radius that the sheet thickness cannot support. These issues are cheaper to resolve on a drawing than on a machined part. For high-frequency designs, the critical dimensions should be identified in the drawing and linked to the manufacturing and inspection plan. A general tolerance block is not enough when a small feature controls the passband or the isolation. Prototype and Design Verification The prototype stage proves that the design can meet the electrical target in hardware. It should include a measured comparison with the simulation, a review of the critical dimensions and a first look at the assembly and test process. If the prototype misses the target, the cause should be identified before the design is revised: a machining error, a material difference, a plating variation and a test-fixture error can all produce the same symptom. Design verification may include temperature, power, PIM and environmental testing, depending on the project. The acceptance criteria should be agreed in advance, and the test setup should be documented so the results can be repeated. A prototype that passes only under a special bench condition is not yet a production design. First Article Inspection First article inspection, or FAI, confirms that the first production-representative part matches the drawing and the approved prototype. It normally covers critical dimensions, material and finish, and the RF performance that the specification requires. The FAI record should identify the drawing revision, the part number, the serial or lot number and the measurement equipment used. The FAI is also the point to confirm the test baseline. The test fixture, calibration, reference plane, limits and data format should be the same ones that will be used in production. If the production test will differ from the prototype test, the correlation between the two should be established before the pilot run. Automated assembly of RF cavity filters. NPI should confirm that the production process, fixtures and test method reproduce the approved prototype, not only that the design is theoretically sound. Pilot Run and Process Capability A pilot run builds a small production batch using the intended process, tooling, fixtures and test flow. Its purpose is to expose the variation that a single prototype cannot show: machining scatter, plating thickness distribution, assembly time, tuning time and test repeatability. The output should be a process that can meet the specification repeatedly, not just a batch that happened to pass. Process capability is evaluated against the critical characteristics. For RF parts, that may mean the passband edges, insertion loss, rejection, return loss, PIM or a critical mechanical dimension. The pilot run should show how those characteristics are distributed and whether the control limits leave enough margin for normal production variation. The pilot also tests the supply chain. Material availability, plating capacity, fixture life and inspection throughput can all become constraints at volume. A pilot run that ignores those constraints may pass technically but fail commercially. Golden Sample and Test Baseline A golden sample is an approved reference unit, or a set of reference data, used to confirm that production test setups remain consistent over time. It is not a substitute for specification limits. It is a correlation tool: if a production unit fails, the golden sample can show whether the unit or the test setup is responsible. The test baseline should include the instrument settings, calibration method, fixture, reference plane and data format. It should also define how often the setup is verified and what happens when a verification fails. For PIM testing, the baseline should include the carrier configuration and the measurement environment because those factors are difficult to reproduce without a documented procedure. Change Control and Mass Production Once the design and process are approved, changes should be controlled. A material substitution, a plating change, a new CNC program, a fixture modification or a supplier change can alter the RF result even when the drawing looks the same. The change control process should identify which changes require a new first article, which require a partial verification and which can be handled by routine inspection. Mass production depends on the same evidence continuing to be generated. Incoming material checks, in-process inspection, final RF test and lot traceability should be defined in the control plan. If a nonconformance appears, the lot or serial number should allow the affected units to be identified and the cause to be investigated. RF NPI Checklist Review the specification for missing or conflicting inputs before design release. Complete a DFM review of tolerances, tool access, plating, assembly and test access. Build a prototype and compare measured performance with the simulation. Agree the verification tests, acceptance criteria and test setup in advance. Complete a first article inspection against the approved drawing and prototype. Run a pilot batch with the intended process, tooling and test flow. Evaluate process capability on the critical RF and mechanical characteristics. Establish a golden sample and a documented test baseline. Define change control, traceability and the production control plan.
